topic.title: Who your RM works for
topic.claim: The relationship manager who calls you 'sir' and remembers your birthday earns more when you buy the product that's worse for you.
topic.moment: The bank RM visits with a 'guaranteed return' plan that is half insurance, half investment.

turn.believed: The RM is the bank's free advisor for me.
turn.actually: The RM is a salesperson with targets, and some products pay far better commissions than others.

topic.feeling: Naive for trusting the friendliest person at the bank.
topic.villain: Cross-sell targets and commission structures inside banks
topic.because: Insurance-linked plans pay higher commissions than a plain FD or index fund. The warmth is real, and so is the target.
topic.payoff: Ask your RM one question: 'What do you earn if I buy this?' Watch how long the answer takes.
topic.behaviour: RMs push ULIPs and endowment plans to salaried customers and to their parents.
topic.mechanism: The product that pays the seller most gets pitched hardest.
topic.group: Salaried account holders and their parents
topic.send_to: Their parents, who just got a call from the bank
topic.why_now: Bonus and year-end tax-saving season is when the RM calls start.
topic.needs_facts: That commissions on insurance-linked products are higher than on plain deposits, from IRDAI or SEBI disclosures

score.why: The friendly bank RM is a salesperson with a target, and the question 'what do you earn?' is a test readers can run. A natural one to send to parents.

topic.title: We read 1-star reviews to buy
topic.claim: We read 1-star reviews to decide to buy, not to avoid. If the complaint is about delivery, we're sold.
topic.moment: You skip the 5 stars and go straight to the angriest review, which says 'box came dented'.

turn.actually: Bad reviews are the only ones we trust, so a harmless complaint works as an endorsement.

topic.feeling: Relieved I finally have a reason to trust something.
topic.villain: Review sections so full of paid praise that only complaints feel real
topic.because: We know 5-star reviews can be bought. A real complaint about a small thing proves the product survived real use.
topic.payoff: The best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier.
topic.behaviour: Shoppers filter by lowest rating first and buy if the flaws are irrelevant to them.
topic.mechanism: Paid praise made complaints the only signal left.
topic.group: Online shoppers who research before buying
topic.send_to: The friend who takes 40 minutes to buy a kettle
topic.why_now: Paid and fake reviews have made star ratings feel useless.

score.why: We go straight to the angriest review, and a harmless complaint ends up working as an endorsement. It's a funny, true habit most people never examine.

topic.title: Only three units left
topic.claim: 'Only three units left at this price' at a site visit is a price ladder, not a shortage.
topic.moment: The sales lady says the price goes up next week, and the cheque book suddenly feels urgent.

turn.actually: Builders release stock in slabs and raise the price each slab, so 'last units' is always true.

topic.feeling: Rushed into the biggest cheque of my life.
topic.villain: Phased inventory releases built into builder pricing
topic.because: Each price step rewards early buyers on paper and pushes late ones to hurry. The builder controls how many units are 'left'.
topic.payoff: Ask how many units are unreleased, not how many are left.
topic.behaviour: Builders announce price hikes by phase and run 'limited' offers at site visits.
topic.send_to: The couple doing site visits every Sunday
topic.why_now: Festive launches just pushed a wave of 'new phase' pricing.

score.why: 'Last units' is always true because the builder controls what's released. The sharp question to ask is how many units are unreleased.

topic.title: The free trial is priced on forgetting
topic.claim: A free trial isn't priced on the people who love the product. It's priced on the people who forget to cancel.
topic.moment: A ₹499 debit in month three for an app you opened twice.

turn.believed: Trials let you test before you pay.
turn.actually: Trials work best for the company when you don't remember them.

topic.villain: Auto-renew subscriptions with cancel buttons buried three screens deep
topic.because: Auto-pay on UPI or card means silence counts as yes. Every forgotten trial is revenue with no service cost.
topic.payoff: Open your UPI autopay list tonight. Count the ones you'd sign up for again today.
topic.behaviour: Apps ask for a mandate up front, then make cancelling harder than joining.
topic.group: Anyone with three or more subscriptions
topic.send_to: The sibling who pays for four OTT apps
topic.why_now: UPI autopay has made signing up one tap and cancelling a hunt.

score.why: A free trial is priced on the people who forget to cancel. The UPI autopay check is a test readers will actually do tonight.

topic.title: The ₹350 chair
topic.claim: Half of what you pay for café coffee is rent on a chair, because our cities have almost nowhere free to sit.
topic.moment: You buy a cold coffee you don't want so you can take a call for an hour.

turn.actually: We're paying for a seat, a plug and Wi-Fi, with the coffee as the ticket.

topic.feeling: Like I'm paying an entry fee to exist in my own city.
topic.villain: Cities with almost no free public places to sit: few libraries, parks or plazas
topic.because: When the only places to sit are ones that sell something, the café can price the seat. The menu is just how it bills you.
topic.payoff: Would you buy that coffee if you could sit in a park with Wi-Fi? Then you know what you paid for.
topic.behaviour: People work, date and take calls from cafés, buying one drink per hour as rent.
topic.mechanism: Scarce free space lets private places charge for sitting.
topic.group: Young professionals in metros, often in shared flats
topic.send_to: The friend who 'works from a café' three days a week
topic.why_now: Hybrid work has filled cafés with laptops on weekdays.
real_details: A r/hyderabad post says the poster doesn't want more cafes and wants clean parks and public spaces instead. The thread text includes no comments, numbers or personal stories.

score.why: The café coffee is the ticket for a chair. Cities with nowhere free to sit explain it, and the line reads as an everyday observation, not a complaint.

topic.title: The photographer runs the wedding
topic.claim: At Indian weddings now, the rituals wait for the photographer, because the album is the part the relatives will actually see.
topic.moment: The pandit pauses the pheras while the camera team asks the couple to 'do that again, slowly'.

turn.actually: They're about the footage, because the reel reaches more people than the venue holds.

topic.feeling: Like a guest at a film shoot.
topic.villain: A wedding industry where the content outlives the event
topic.because: The reel gets shown for years and travels further than the event. So the timeline is built around light and angles.
topic.payoff: At the next wedding, watch who says 'one more time'. That's the person in charge.
topic.behaviour: Couples book the photo team first and plan rituals around golden hour and drone shots.
topic.mechanism: Footage reaches more people than the event.
topic.group: People going to or planning weddings this season
topic.send_to: The friend getting married in December

score.why: The rituals wait for the camera because the reel outlives the venue. It fits 'weddings are for the relatives' with a funny, fresh turn.

topic.title: Diwali has one film
topic.claim: At Diwali the family picks one film and every other release loses, because a festival ticket is a group decision and not a taste decision.
topic.behaviour: Families book seats together and choose what everyone, including the grandmother, can sit through. The weekend chart was lopsided: Ramayana took ₹174.00 crore of the top five's ₹252.75 crore net, and Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.
topic.mechanism: Theatres give shows to whatever fills the hall, and groups fill the hall for the film that is safe for all ages. A hit gets more screens, which makes it look even bigger.
topic.group: People who go to the movies with family at festival time
topic.moment: You wanted to see a different film this Diwali, but the family plan had one name on it.

turn.believed: The biggest film wins because it is the best film.
turn.actually: It wins because a group of different ages can agree on it, and screens then follow the crowd.

topic.feeling: Part of a crowd and slightly left out of your own choice
topic.villain: A screen-allocation system that rewards whatever fills the hall in the first weekend
topic.because: Exhibitors earn from full halls, so they move shows to the film families choose. The second-choice film loses its place even if people liked it.

proof.fact: Sacnilk puts the top five films at ₹252.75 crore net for the Diwali weekend, with Ramayana taking ₹174.00 Cr (69% of that). Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.

topic.payoff: A festival hit is the film the whole family could say yes to, not necessarily the one anyone loved most.
topic.send_to: The friend who always ends up watching what the family picks
real_details: Scene grew on both Saturday and Sunday, unlike the usual front-loaded star release
topic.news_peg: Sacnilk's Diwali weekend (November 6-8) box office report (2026-11-09)
topic.why_now: The Diwali weekend numbers have just come out.

score.why: A festival ticket is a group decision, not a taste decision. The box-office fact supports the argument instead of being the point.
